title: Minimax games for quantum channel discrimination
authors: Kun Fang, Michael X. Cao, Hao-Chung Cheng, Li Gao, Masahito Hayashi
abstract: Quantum channel discrimination is a primitive task for identifying, verifying, and benchmarking quantum dynamics. Previous studies have primarily considered either the best-case tester-input setting or the worst-case jammer-input setting. Here, we introduce a game-theoretic framework in which both the tester and jammer control separate inputs. Combining three input structures, characterized by whether the tester and jammer use entangled inputs or IID inputs across channel uses, with four information patterns, determined by the visibility of the jammer's strategy and its knowledge of the true hypothesis, yields twelve game models. We provide exact finite blocklength hypothesis testing characterizations of all twelve models in terms of nine minimax hypothesis testing divergences and derive their asymptotic Stein exponents. Notably, for entangled jammers, neither the visibility of the jammer's strategy nor its knowledge of the true hypothesis affects the asymptotic Stein exponent, whereas the information pattern remains consequential for IID jammers. As an example, we study the discrimination of a general channel from a replacer channel and show that all asymptotic Stein exponents coincide with the same additive, single letter quantity. We further develop a general argument that upgrades achievability results to strong converse results, thereby establishing strong converse properties for several game models, resolving an open problem in composite hypothesis testing posed by Berta et al. [Commun. Math. Phys. 385, 55 (2021)], and strengthening several recent results of Lami [arXiv:2510.06340]. The framework and techniques developed here may support future studies of quantum information tasks involving competing roles.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive minimax game-theoretic framework to analyze quantum channel discrimination, treating the problem as a game between a tester and a jammer. By combining input structures and information patterns, the authors derive exact characterizations and asymptotic exponents for twelve distinct models. This advances the understanding of fundamental limits in quantum hypothesis testing and resolves several open problems in the field.
main_problem: The paper addresses quantum channel discrimination, which is a fundamental task for verifying quantum dynamics, by developing a comprehensive game-theoretic framework.
main_result: It characterizes the asymptotic Stein exponents for twelve distinct minimax game models, establishing strong converse properties for several previously open problems in composite hypothesis testing.
method: The authors employ a minimax game-theoretic approach, combining input structures (entangled vs. IID) with information patterns (visibility and hypothesis awareness) to derive exact finite blocklength characterizations using minimax hypothesis testing divergences.
model_or_system: The system involves distinguishing between candidate quantum channels ($\mathcal{G}$) using inputs controlled by both a tester and a jammer in a game-theoretic setting.
key_observables: Asymptotic Stein exponents, minimax hypothesis testing divergences, and error probabilities ($\alpha_T,  eta_T$).
important_parameters: Blocklength ($n$), error tolerance ($\epsilon$), and the structure of the inputs (entangled vs. IID).
main_assumptions: The framework analyzes twelve specific game models derived from combinations of input structures and information patterns; some results rely on specific assumptions regarding the jammer's input preparation.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the three input configurations (Tester, Jammer, Minimax). Figure 2 details the four information patterns based on jammer visibility and hypothesis awareness. Table 1 summarizes the twelve resulting Stein exponents.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general minimax game-theoretic framework for channel discrimination. It then analyzes the resulting twelve models, deriving exact characterizations and asymptotic exponents. Finally, it develops general arguments to upgrade achievability to strong converse results, resolving specific open problems.
why_interesting: The rigorous game-theoretic modeling of adversarial quantum tasks, especially the derivation of strong converse bounds, provides powerful tools applicable to understanding the fundamental limits of quantum communication and verification protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Tester-input, jammer-input, and minimax-input configurations. The central grey box G denotes the channel under test. Tester systems are shown in blue, and jammer systems in orange. In (a), the tester controls the channel input and final test, while the jammer input is absent. In (b), the jammer controls the channel input, while the tester performs the final test and has no input control. In (c), the tester and jammer control separate channel inputs, and the tester performs the final test.

Figure 2: Four information patterns of the jammer. Rows indicate whether the jammer’s input-selection rule is public or secret, while columns indicate whether the jammer is hypothesis-unaware or hypothesis- aware. In the public row, the dashed orange arrow denotes that the jammer’s rule is disclosed before the tester acts. In the hypothesis-aware column, the jammer may use σ when N is active and ω when M is active; in the hypothesis-unaware column, it must use the same state τ under both hypotheses.

Figure 3: Three input structures for n parallel channel uses. The tester’s systems are shown in blue and the jammer’s systems in orange. In (a), both players may prepare entangled inputs. In (b), the tester is restricted to IID inputs, whereas the jammer may still prepare entangled inputs. In (c), both players are restricted to IID inputs. All tests are performed on the tester’s systems and can be entangled.

Figure 4: Summary of the main results. At finite blocklength, the twelve game models reduce to nine hypothesis-testing divergences (Definition 12). Asymptotically, they reduce to five Umegaki relative entropy rates (Definition 14). Solid and dashed connectors indicate strong- and weak-converse results, respectively. For a replacer alternative, all Stein exponents reduce to the same single-letter value.
